definitionEn: the series of jobs in a person's working life.
existingExample: Few people now follow a single career path.

definitionEn: moving to a higher position at work.
existingExample: She gained a promotion after two years.

definitionEn: an unofficial barrier stopping women or minorities reaching top jobs.
existingExample: Few women have broken through the glass ceiling in banking.

definitionEn: the difference between men's and women's average pay.
existingExample: Some governments require large companies to publish their gender pay gap.

definitionEn: time off work for a mother before and after childbirth.
existingExample: Generous maternity leave helps keep women in the workforce.

definitionEn: time off work for a new father.
existingExample: More fathers are now taking paternity leave.

definitionEn: extra benefits such as health insurance or a company car.
existingExample: Fringe benefits can matter more than salary to some employees.

definitionEn: money paid regularly after retirement.
existingExample: An ageing population puts pressure on state pensions.

definitionEn: the age at which people stop working.
existingExample: Several countries have raised the retirement age.

definitionEn: working for several clients rather than one employer.
existingExample: A growing number of experienced graphic designers choose to work freelance to enjoy greater autonomy over their schedules.

definitionEn: working for yourself rather than for an employer.
existingExample: Self-employed workers usually do not receive sick pay.

definitionEn: a contract with no guaranteed minimum hours.
meaningVi: hợp đồng không cam kết giờ làm
existingExample: Zero-hours contracts leave workers with unpredictable incomes.

definitionEn: worry about losing your job.
existingExample: Job insecurity can damage workers' mental health.

definitionEn: not secure or stable.
existingExample: Many young people are trapped in precarious employment.

definitionEn: to stop employing someone because there is no work.
existingExample: During a severe recession, struggling manufacturing firms are often forced to lay off hundreds of experienced workers.

definitionEn: reducing the number of employees in an organisation.
existingExample: Downsizing left the remaining staff overworked.

definitionEn: the amount of work someone has to do.
existingExample: Teachers complain of an increasingly heavy workload.

definitionEn: time worked beyond normal hours.
existingExample: Many employees regularly work unpaid overtime.

definitionEn: working while ill or staying late only to appear committed.
meaningVi: đi làm khi không đủ sức khỏe/hiệu quả
existingExample: Presenteeism can spread illness and reduce productivity.

definitionEn: how committed and enthusiastic staff are.
meaningVi: mức độ gắn kết của nhân viên
existingExample: Recognition boosts employee engagement.

definitionEn: the confidence and enthusiasm of a group.
existingExample: Pay cuts severely damaged staff morale.

definitionEn: the rate at which employees leave and are replaced.
meaningVi: tỷ lệ thay đổi nhân sự
existingExample: High staff turnover is costly for employers.

definitionEn: a belief in the value of hard work.
existingExample: Employers value candidates with a strong work ethic.

definitionEn: a lack of workers with the skills employers need.
existingExample: The construction industry faces a severe skills shortage.

definitionEn: keeping staff from leaving an organisation.
existingExample: Flexible working improves employee retention.

definitionEn: the activity of setting up businesses.
existingExample: Tax breaks can encourage entrepreneurship.

definitionEn: a newly established business.
existingExample: Most start-ups fail within their first few years.

definitionEn: money invested in new businesses with high risk.
existingExample: The start-up raised venture capital to expand abroad.

definitionEn: the percentage of a market a company controls.
existingExample: The brand lost market share to cheaper rivals.

definitionEn: an advantage over competitors.
existingExample: Innovation gives firms a competitive edge.

definitionEn: the relationship between how much is available and how much is wanted.
existingExample: Prices are largely determined by supply and demand.

definitionEn: money spent by households on goods and services.
existingExample: Consumer spending fell sharply during the recession.

definitionEn: how much money can buy.
existingExample: Inflation erodes the purchasing power of savings.

definitionEn: a wage high enough to cover basic living costs.
existingExample: Campaigners want all employers to pay a living wage.

definitionEn: wages not rising over time.
existingExample: Wage stagnation has squeezed middle-income families.

definitionEn: a period when economic activity falls.
existingExample: Luxury brands suffer during an economic downturn.

definitionEn: a period of rapid economic growth.
existingExample: The property boom made housing unaffordable for many.

definitionEn: government cuts in public spending.
meaningVi: chính sách thắt lưng buộc bụng
existingExample: Austerity measures led to cuts in public services.

definitionEn: government decisions on taxation and spending.
existingExample: Fiscal policy can be used to stimulate the economy.

definitionEn: government spending designed to encourage economic activity.
existingExample: The government launched a stimulus package to protect jobs.

definitionEn: illegally avoiding paying taxes.
existingExample: Tax evasion deprives public services of funds.

definitionEn: legally reducing the tax you pay by using loopholes.
meaningVi: né thuế (lợi dụng kẽ hở luật)
existingExample: Multinationals have been criticised for aggressive tax avoidance.

definitionEn: a system in which higher earners pay a larger percentage.
existingExample: Progressive taxation helps reduce inequality.

definitionEn: a system in which the government provides social support.
existingExample: The welfare state provides healthcare, pensions and benefits.

definitionEn: government support that prevents people falling into poverty.
existingExample: Unemployment benefits are part of the social safety net.

definitionEn: money paid to people who have no job.
existingExample: Some argue that generous unemployment benefits discourage work.

definitionEn: the difference in wealth between rich and poor.
existingExample: The wealth gap has widened in many countries.

definitionEn: the theory that benefits for the rich eventually reach everyone.
existingExample: Critics argue that trickle-down economics rarely helps the poor.

definitionEn: trade between countries without taxes or limits.
existingExample: Free trade agreements have boosted the country's exports.

definitionEn: protecting domestic industry by taxing imports.
meaningVi: chủ nghĩa bảo hộ mậu dịch
existingExample: Protectionism can lead to higher prices for consumers.

definitionEn: a tax on imported goods.
existingExample: The government imposed tariffs on imported steel.

definitionEn: a situation where a country imports more than it exports.
existingExample: The country has a large trade deficit with its neighbour.

definitionEn: the total value of goods and services produced in a country.
existingExample: GDP per capita is often used to compare living standards.

definitionEn: for each person.
existingExample: Income per capita has doubled in two decades.

definitionEn: a country experiencing rapid growth and industrialisation.
existingExample: As an emerging economy, the country has attracted substantial foreign investment while rapidly modernising its infrastructure.

definitionEn: investment by a foreign company in businesses in another country.
meaningVi: đầu tư trực tiếp nước ngoài
existingExample: Low labour costs helped attract foreign direct investment.

definitionEn: the part of the economy that makes goods.
existingExample: The manufacturing sector has shrunk in many Western countries.

definitionEn: the part of the economy that provides services.
existingExample: Most jobs in wealthy countries are now in the service sector.

definitionEn: making you feel satisfied and useful.
existingExample: Many people prefer a fulfilling job to a high salary.

definitionEn: giving satisfaction.
existingExample: Teaching can be an extremely rewarding career.

definitionEn: boring because it never changes.
existingExample: Automation can take over monotonous tasks.

definitionEn: to learn new skills for work.
existingExample: Companies need to upskill workers to use AI tools.

definitionEn: to train people for a different job.
meaningVi: đào tạo kỹ năng mới (cho nghề khác)
existingExample: Governments should reskill workers displaced by automation.

definitionEn: splitting working time between home and the office.
meaningVi: làm việc kết hợp (nhà + văn phòng)
existingExample: Hybrid working has become the norm in many offices.

definitionEn: negotiations between unions and employers about pay and conditions.
existingExample: Unions secure pay rises through collective bargaining.

definitionEn: an organisation representing workers' interests.
existingExample: Trade unions campaign for better working conditions.

definitionEn: action by workers, such as strikes, to protest.
existingExample: Nurses took industrial action over pay.

definitionEn: a risk that comes with a particular job.
existingExample: Back pain is an occupational hazard for builders.

definitionEn: to share something out again, usually more fairly.
existingExample: Higher taxes on the rich can be used to redistribute wealth.

definitionEn: the gradual loss of employees who leave and are not replaced.
meaningVi: tỷ lệ nhân viên nghỉ việc
existingExample: Better working conditions can reduce staff attrition.

definitionEn: regularly staying away from work or school without good reason.
meaningVi: tình trạng nghỉ làm thường xuyên
existingExample: Flexible schedules have helped reduce absenteeism.

definitionEn: to take the place of someone or something, forcing them out.
existingExample: Some workers fear they will be displaced by automation.

definitionEn: to happen or appear as expected or predicted.
existingExample: The promised economic benefits never materialised.

definitionEn: a tendency that makes results or judgements unfair or inaccurate.
existingExample: Self-reported data can carry a risk of bias.

definitionEn: increases in how much is produced per worker or per hour.
existingExample: New technology often brings productivity gains, but not always higher wages.

definitionEn: to try hard to deal with a difficult problem.
existingExample: Rapidly growing megacities must grapple with severe shortages of affordable housing.

definitionEn: to measure or judge something, especially feelings or results.
existingExample: Surveys are used to gauge public opinion.

definitionEn: A persistent economic condition combining sluggish growth, elevated unemployment, and stubbornly high price inflation.
meaningVi: tình trạng lạm phát đình trệ
existingExample: Central bankers dread prolonged stagflation because raising interest rates cools inflation yet risks deepening job losses.

definitionEn: A sustained decline in the general price level of goods and services, often discouraging spending and investment.
existingExample: Economists caution that entrenched deflation can paralyse consumption as households postpone major purchases expecting lower prices.

definitionEn: Rapid, out-of-control escalation of general prices that destroys public confidence in a national currency.
meaningVi: siêu lạm phát làm đồng tiền mất giá nghiêm trọng
existingExample: Unrestrained money printing during severe fiscal crises has historically triggered hyperinflation, wiping out ordinary citizens' life savings.

definitionEn: Actions taken by a central bank to regulate money supply, credit conditions, and benchmark interest rates.
meaningVi: chính sách tiền tệ do ngân hàng trung ương điều hành
existingExample: Tightening monetary policy remains the primary mechanism for cooling overheated housing markets without altering parliamentary tax laws.

definitionEn: An unconventional central-bank policy of purchasing government bonds and financial assets to inject liquidity into a stalled economy.
meaningVi: nới lỏng định lượng bơm thanh khoản qua mua trái phiếu
existingExample: While quantitative easing stabilised commercial credit after the financial crash, critics argue it disproportionately inflated asset prices.

definitionEn: The total financial obligations borrowed by a national government through treasury bonds and international creditors.
meaningVi: nợ công quốc gia do chính phủ phát hành hoặc bảo lãnh
existingExample: Escalating borrowing costs have forced several heavily indebted nations to restructure their sovereign debt under international supervision.

definitionEn: A budgetary shortfall occurring when a government's total annual expenditures exceed its tax and non-tax revenues.
meaningVi: thâm hụt ngân sách nhà nước khi chi tiêu vượt nguồn thu
existingExample: Sustaining a wide fiscal deficit during periods of strong growth leaves treasuries with limited headroom during future recessions.

definitionEn: A fiscal state in which public revenues surpass government expenditures over a designated accounting period.
meaningVi: thặng dư ngân sách khi nguồn thu vượt tổng chi tiêu công
existingExample: Resource-rich countries that channel a temporary budget surplus into sovereign wealth funds better cushion future commodity downturns.

definitionEn: The ease and speed with which financial assets can be converted into cash without significantly losing market value.
meaningVi: tính thanh khoản (mức độ chuyển đổi nhanh chóng sang tiền mặt)
existingExample: Small exporters frequently collapse during sudden credit freezes not from poor products, but from acute short-term liquidity shortages.

definitionEn: A state of financial distress in which a business or individual cannot pay debts as they fall due.
meaningVi: tình trạng mất khả năng thanh toán nợ đến hạn
existingExample: Reforming corporate insolvency frameworks allows viable struggling firms to reorganise debts rather than liquidate abruptly.

definitionEn: A market structure dominated by a small handful of powerful firms whose pricing decisions strongly influence the entire industry.
meaningVi: độc quyền nhóm bị chi phối bởi một vài doanh nghiệp
existingExample: Consumer watchdogs warn that the domestic telecommunications oligopoly keeps mobile data tariffs artificially high.

definitionEn: An association of competing producers that collude to fix prices, restrict output, or divide markets to boost profits.
meaningVi: liên minh độc quyền thông đồng ấn định giá bán
existingExample: Competition authorities imposed record fines after uncovering a clandestine construction cartel rigging municipal bridge tenders.

definitionEn: Relating to statutes and regulatory enforcement aimed at curbing monopolistic practices and preserving open market competition.
meaningVi: chống độc quyền nhằm bảo vệ cạnh tranh công bằng
existingExample: Lawmakers are updating twentieth-century antitrust legislation to scrutinise how digital platforms acquire emerging rivals.

definitionEn: The reduction or elimination of government rules and oversight governing a particular commercial industry.
meaningVi: quá trình bãi bỏ hoặc nới lỏng các quy định kiểm soát
existingExample: While airline deregulation lowered regional ticket fares, unchecked financial deregulation contributed directly to systemic banking fragility.

definitionEn: The transfer of state-owned enterprises, utilities, or public assets into private commercial ownership and operation.
meaningVi: tư nhân hóa tài sản hoặc doanh nghiệp nhà nước
existingExample: Public debate over water-utility privatisation centres on whether profit incentives undermine long-term maintenance of vital pipes.

definitionEn: The process by which a government assumes public ownership and operational control over a previously private industry.
meaningVi: quốc hữu hóa chuyển giao ngành kinh tế về nhà nước
existingExample: Following repeated rail operator failures, commuter groups campaigned vigorously for the gradual nationalisation of regional train lines.

definitionEn: An economy's capacity to produce specific goods or services at a lower opportunity cost than its trading partners.
meaningVi: lợi thế so sánh trong sản xuất nhờ chi phí cơ hội thấp
existingExample: Classical trade theory maintains that nations prosper mutually when each specialises according to its distinct comparative advantage.

definitionEn: Cost advantages attained by enterprises as production volume expands, spreading fixed expenses across greater output.
meaningVi: lợi thế kinh tế theo quy mô giúp giảm chi phí đơn vị
existingExample: Massive battery gigafactories achieve formidable economies of scale that have rapidly lowered electric-vehicle sticker prices.

definitionEn: The economic principle that adding successive units of one input eventually yields progressively smaller increments of output.
meaningVi: quy luật lợi suất giảm dần khi tăng một yếu tố đầu vào
existingExample: Expanding motorway lanes indefinitely soon encounters diminishing returns as induced traffic quickly refills newly added capacity.

definitionEn: An unpriced side effect of production or consumption that imposes costs or confers benefits on uninvolved third parties.
existingExample: Congestion pricing is designed to internalise the negative externality of urban air pollution caused by private commuter cars.

definitionEn: A situation in which unregulated free markets fail to allocate goods, services, or public resources efficiently for society.
meaningVi: thất bại thị trường khi cơ chế tự do phân bổ kém hiệu quả
existingExample: Underinvestment in preventative vaccines is a textbook market failure that justifies direct public research subsidies.

definitionEn: The tendency of an institution or individual to take excessive risks when shielded from bearing the full financial consequences.
existingExample: Unconditional taxpayer bailouts for reckless investment banks create acute moral hazard by rewarding speculative excess.

definitionEn: A market condition in which one party to an economic transaction possesses substantially more relevant knowledge than the other.
meaningVi: thông tin bất cân xứng giữa các bên tham gia giao dịch
existingExample: Mandatory nutritional labels and financial disclosures help reduce asymmetric information between corporations and ordinary consumers.
